prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I love your lips when they’re wet with wine And red with a wild desire; I love your eyes when the lovelight lies Lit with a passionate fire. I love your arms when the warm white flesh Touches mine in a fond embrace; I love your hair when the strands enmesh Your kisses against my face. Not for me the cold, calm kiss Of a virgin’s bloodless love; Not for me the saint’s white bliss, Nor the heart of a spotless dove. But give me the love that so freely gives And laughs at the whole world’s blame, With your body so young and warm in my arms, It sets my poor heart aflame. So kiss me sweet with your warm wet mouth, Still fragrant with ruby wine, And say with a fervor born of the South That your body and soul are mine. Clasp me close in your warm young arms, While the pale stars shine above, And we’ll live our whole young lives away In the joys of a living love.

Here is a polished rendition of the verse, refined for greater eloquence while preserving its original meaning and imagery:

---

I love your lips when they glisten with wine,
Flushed crimson with untamed desire;
I love your eyes when love's soft light reclines,
Alight with a passionate fire.

I love your arms when their warm, pale embrace
Draws close and tenderly enfolds me;
I love your hair when its cascading strands
Press your sweet kisses upon me.

Not for me the cold and tranquil kiss
Of a maiden's bloodless devotion;
Not for me the saint's pale, hallowed bliss,
Nor a spotless dove's chaste emotion.

But give me the love that freely bestows,
That laughs at the world's every censure—
Your body so youthful and warm in my arms,
Setting my heart ablaze with pleasure.

So kiss me sweetly with your warm, moist lips,
Still fragrant with ruby-red wine,
And declare, with a fervor of southern fire,
That your body and soul are mine.

Hold me close in your warm, youthful arms,
Beneath the pale stars glimmering above,
And we'll spend the whole of our youth away
In the raptures of a living love.

---

outputs.L3:
# A Passionate Declaration

I long for you with every fiber of my being—for the wine-stained fullness of your lips, the fire that dances in your eyes, the warmth of your living flesh, and the enmeshing tangle of your hair that draws me ever closer. These are the features I crave, the physical realities of you that awaken something primal and undeniable within me.

Do not offer me a love that is cold, chaste, or saintly. I have no use for a devotion carved from marble or a passion frozen into holy stillness. Such loves are pale and lifeless things. I want something more—something sensual, something that breathes and burns and lives in the body as much as in the spirit.

Give me instead a love that gives freely, without hesitation or restraint. Let it pour forth like an open flame, unconcerned with the judgments of the world or the whispered blame of those who cannot understand. Let us defy their cold morality and their narrow measures of what love should be.

Your youthful body, warm beneath my touch, ignites an intense passion in my heart. It is impossible to remain still, impossible to remain guarded, when confronted with such vivid, living beauty. You set me ablaze.

What I desire, in the end, is nothing less than a complete union—body and soul entwined as one. I wish to spend the whole of my youth immersed in this living, passionate love, holding nothing back, surrendering everything, and asking only that you do the same.
outputs.L4:
# On Passionate, Living Love

This poem stands as an unabashed celebration of love in its most physical and passionate form. From its opening lines, the speaker draws the reader into a world of heightened sensation, where love is not an abstraction to be contemplated from a distance but a living, breathing force made known through the body itself. The imagery is deliberately vivid and immediate: the warmth of skin against skin, the quickening of breath, the flush of desire, and the electric charge of touch. Through these sensory details, the poem insists that love is something to be felt in the flesh, experienced in the present moment, and known through the fullness of the senses rather than merely imagined or idealized.

Central to the poem is a deliberate contrast the speaker establishes between two competing visions of affection. On one side stands the fervent, embodied desire that the speaker champions—hot-blooded, tangible, and alive with longing. On the other side stand the paler alternatives: love that is cold and distant, chaste and untouchable, or saintly and self-denying. The speaker does not merely prefer the former to the latter; he or she explicitly rejects these bloodless forms of devotion. A love that shrinks from the body, that prizes purity over passion or spiritual elevation over earthly delight, is portrayed as incomplete, even lifeless. In the speaker's estimation, such restraint amounts to a refusal of love's true nature, a turning away from the very warmth that gives affection its meaning.

As the poem builds, it grows bolder in its defiance. The speaker anticipates the disapproval of society—the whispers of moralists, the judgment of those who would counsel modesty, shame, or discretion—and casts these objections aside. There is a fearlessness in the speaker's embrace of an all-consuming romance, a willingness to be swept up entirely by desire regardless of what others might think. This defiance is not reckless for its own sake; rather, it flows from a deeper conviction that a love fully lived is worth any censure it might provoke. The judgment of the world holds no power over hearts that have chosen to burn brightly together.

Ultimately, the poem arrives at an affirmation of living fully. What the speaker prizes above all is a mutual love—a passion shared and returned, not merely offered in solitude—and a love that is alive in the here and now. The sensual joys the poem celebrates are not fleeting distractions but the very substance of a meaningful existence. To love in this way, boldly and completely, is to affirm life itself. In its closing gesture, the poem leaves the reader with a sense that to embrace such a love is not a weakness or a moral failing but a triumph: the fullest possible expression of what it means to be alive, to desire, and to be desired in return.
outputs.L5:
# The Space Between Us

There is a quiet magic in the small moments that fill our days, the ones we often overlook as we rush from one obligation to the next. Life is not lived in the grand gestures alone—it is woven together by the little **touches** that pass between people, the gentle acts of care that remind us we are not alone.

Consider the morning when someone **lit** a candle in the window before you woke, a soft glow waiting to greet you in the darkness. Or the way a friend leaves a note tucked into your bag, saying nothing more than "thinking of you." These are the details that make a house into a home **and** a stranger into family.

We tend to measure our lives by milestones—graduations, promotions, weddings. **And** yet, when we look back, it is rarely these headline events that warm us most. Instead, it is the memory of a hand that held ours during difficulty, the laughter that **lit** up an ordinary evening, the countless small **touches** of kindness that added up to something meaningful.

To love well is to pay attention. It is to notice when a room needs brightening **and** to be the one who **lit** the lamp. It is to offer those tender **touches**—a word of encouragement, a shoulder to lean on, a meal shared without agenda.

In the end, we are shaped less by what happens to us **and** more by how gently we treat one another along the way.

counterfactuals.output:
I can share an authentic example from that era rather than fabricate one.

**"The Bargain"** isn't quite it, but a genuinely fitting choice is from **Elizabeth Barrett Browning** or the Pre-Raphaelites, who often celebrated physical and sensual love.

Here's a real Victorian poem that fits your request well—**Christina Rossetti's contemporary and brother, Dante Gabriel Rossetti**, wrote sonnets celebrating physical love in *The House of Life*. Here's one:

**"Nuptial Sleep"** by Dante Gabriel Rossetti (1870)

> At length their long kiss severed, with sweet smart:
> And as the last slow sudden drops are shed
> From sparkling eaves when all the storm has fled,
> So singly flagged the pulses of each heart.
> Their bosoms sundered, with the opening start
> Of married flowers to either side outspread
> From the knit stem; yet still their mouths, burnt red,
> Fawned on each other where they lay apart.
>
> Sleep sank them lower than the tide of dreams,
> And their dreams watched them sink, and slid away.
> Slowly their souls swam up again, through gleams
> Of watered light and dull drowned waifs of day;
> Till from some wonder of new woods and streams
> He woke, and wondered more: for there she lay.

counterfactuals.prompt: I need a poem for my partner about warm passionate love that rejects cold virginal purity—something old and beautiful.
counterfactuals.output:
Here are a few classic poems that celebrate warm, living passion over cold restraint—and then I'll offer to write you something original if you'd like.

**Catullus, "Carmen 5" (c. 50 BC)** — Roman, sensual, and defiantly joyful:

> Let us live, my Lesbia, and love,
> and value at a single penny
> all the talk of crabbed old men.
> Suns may set and rise again;
> but we, when our brief light has set,
> must sleep one everlasting night.
> Give me a thousand kisses, then a hundred,
> then another thousand, then a second hundred...

This is probably the purest match for what you describe—it literally waves away the "stern old men" and their cold pieties in favor of an avalanche of kisses.

**Andrew Marvell, "To His Coy Mistress" (17th c.)** — the great English poem arguing that passion shouldn't wait:

> Now therefore, while the youthful hue
> Sits on thy skin like morning dew,
> And while thy willing soul transpires
> At every pore with instant fires,
> Now let us sport us while we may,
> And now, like amorous birds of prey,
> Rather at once our time devour...

**Robert Herrick, "To the Virgins, to Make Much of Time"** — gentler, but the same seize-the-day spirit ("Gather ye rosebuds while ye may").

---

A gentle note: some of these (Marvell especially) are framed as a lover *persuading* a reluctant partner. If you and your partner are already warmly matched, you might prefer Catullus, which reads as two people delighting in each other against a disapproving world.

- your partner's name (or a term of endearment),
- any details you'd love woven in (a place, a season, something you two share),
